55+ manufactured-home parks in BC: named examples

This is a representative set, not a full list. Each park below was verified by name from a public source that states its age restriction. Pad rents and fees are listing-stated for one home on one date, not a park tariff, so confirm them with the park.
Westwood Estates — 8254 134 St, Surrey (Queen Mary Park Surrey)

MLS listings describe "WESTWOOD ESTATES, 55+ age restricted", a gated manufactured-home park; one listing states a pad rent of $935 per month including the land portion of property taxes, garbage pickup, sewer and water, and that large dogs are allowed with park approval.
Newton Mobile Home Park — 6571 King George Blvd, Surrey (West Newton)

A park directory describes it as an age-restricted (55+) manufactured-home community and a land-lease community with a total of 34 home sites; MLS listings for homes in the park describe a "quiet 55+ community", subject to park approval, with no strata fees. The directory's lot-rent range carries its own warning that lot rent can change without notice — confirm the current pad rent with the park.
Val Maria (Val Maria Manufactured Home Park) — 21163 Lougheed Highway, Maple Ridge (Southwest Maple Ridge)

MLS listings repeatedly describe "VAL MARIA, 55+ age restricted manufactured home park" / "55+ age restricted park"; one listing states a monthly pad rent of $601.90 including the land portion of property taxes, garbage pickup, sewer and water, with 2 small pets allowed — listing-stated for that home; pad rents vary by home and date in the listings checked, so confirm the figure for the specific site.
Pinecrest Mobile Home Park (Pinecrest MHP) — 12022 Pretty Road, Lake Country (Okanagan)

REALTOR.ca and brokerage listings describe "Pinecrest a cozy MHP" where the "Park is 55+", a "quiet, friendly over 55 Park", behind the Lakewood Mall / Lakewood Mall area of Lake Country; one listing states pad fees include water, sewer and snow removal. Title for homes in the park is recorded as leasehold in a REALTOR.ca property summary.
Cultus Lake Village — 3942 Columbia Valley Road, Cultus Lake (Fraser Valley, near Chilliwack)

A listing for a home in the park describes "Cultus Lake Village, a welcoming 55+ community" and a "family-owned and operated park for over 25 years", walking distance to Cultus Lake. Park size: UNCONFIRMED from the sources checked.
Pioneer Park — 27111 0 Ave, Langley / Aldergrove (Township of Langley)

A 55+ manufactured-home co-operative: MLS listings state "Pioneer Park is 55+", that a buyer must be accepted by the co-op and purchase co-op shares (one listing: $9,200, refunded upon sale) and pay monthly co-op fees ($510 in the same listing) rather than pad rent. Because the land is held through the co-operative, this is not a standard Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act pad tenancy — confirm the tenure documents with the co-op.
Sea Ridge Bays — 15875 20 Ave, Surrey (South Surrey / King George Corridor)

A 55+ manufactured-home community that is a bare-land strata: MLS property data records "Age Restricted 55+" in its bylaws restrictions, and listings state "Sea Ridge Bays is 55+", "NO PAD FEES", and that as a bare-land strata "YOU OWN THE LOT", with a monthly strata fee ($210 in the listings, including water) instead of pad rent. Strata law, not the park tenancy Act, is the frame here.

Check each park yourself. Breakaway Bays in South Surrey produced conflicting age claims in the sources, and Crispen Bays and Crestway Bays on King George Boulevard are listed as all-ages, so a park’s age label cannot be assumed from its city.
BC rules for park tenancies and 55+ parks
The governing statute is the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act (MHPTA)

It applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on; a home on land the owner also owns is dealt with through the land title system instead, and if a person rents both the home and the site from an owner, the Residential Tenancy Act — not the MHPTA — applies.
The 55+ rule in a park is a park designation, not a strata bylaw

The Province states the general rule for a designated 55-plus park: at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. Individual parks can state their occupancy rule more strictly in their own documents — one Aldergrove co-op listing states both occupants must be 55 — so the park's own tenancy agreement and rules are the operative document, not the strata age-bylaw regime (Strata Property Act ss. 123.1/123.2 applies to strata corporations, not to pad tenancies).
Buying in a park is an assignment, not a new tenancy

When a home in a park is sold, the buyer does not get a new tenancy — the existing pad tenancy agreement is assigned to the purchaser. Before the seller asks the park owner to consent, the seller must give the proposed purchaser a copy of any written part of the tenancy agreement and any written park rules that apply to the tenancy.
Park owner consent and the 10-day rule

assignment needs the park owner's prior written consent (or consent deemed given, or an order of the director). The request is made in writing on the approved form (RTB Form 10), the park owner must respond so the home owner receives the response by the 10th day after the request is received, and if there is no response by the end of the 10th day, consent is deemed to have been given; the park owner must not charge a fee or receive a benefit for giving consent. On assignment, the purchaser becomes the tenant of the park owner and assumes the rights and obligations under the Act and the tenancy agreement from the assignment date, on the same terms as before.
Pad rent increases — the allowable formula

a landlord may increase pad rent once every 12 months, with at least 3 full months' notice, and the increase is capped by formula — the inflation rate (the 12-month average change in the BC all-items Consumer Price Index) plus a proportional amount (the change in local government levies plus the change in regulated park utilities, divided by the number of manufactured home sites in the park). The formula is set in the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Regulation.
Park rules

park rules are part of the tenancy agreement; a rule is enforceable only if it applies to all tenants fairly, is clear enough for a reasonable tenant to follow, is properly noticed, and does not change a material term of the tenancy agreement. Since the April 30, 2024 regulation change, park rules can only be changed once a year and with three months' notice —.
Park closure or redevelopment

a landlord converting all or a significant part of a park to a non-residential use, or to a residential use other than a manufactured home park, must have all necessary government permits and approvals in place before issuing notice, must give a 12-month notice to end tenancy, and must pay the tenant $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date; a tenant may move out early on at least 10 days' written notice, paying rent to the move-out date.
Registration of the home itself — the Manufactured Home Registry

a sale, transfer or purchase of a manufactured home is only effective if registered in the Manufactured Home Registry, the province's central register of manufactured home ownership, administered through BC Registries. On a sale, the original signed Bill of Sale and the Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership are filed through a qualified supplier (a lawyer or notary), and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale.
Property tax and the Home Owner Grant

a manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential property owners, and the assessed value does not include the value of the land when the home is in a manufactured home park not on reserve land, or on land privately owned by someone other than the home owner. A manufactured home occupied as a principal residence by its registered owner can qualify for the Home Owner Grant, applied for each year.
Municipal layer

there is no province-wide park zoning — each municipality zones manufactured home parks in its own bylaw — and some cities add a park-redevelopment policy on top of the Act; Surrey's Manufactured Home Park Policy brochure, for example, walks residents through the 12-month notice, permits-first and $20,000 compensation steps and names help organizations including the BC Manufactured Home Owners association and the Tenant Resource & Advisory Centre.

faq.q: If I buy a mobile home in a park, do I own the land?
faq.a: No. You own the home and rent the site under a pad tenancy agreement; the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on.

faq.q: Can the park owner refuse to let me buy a home in the park?
faq.a: The sale needs the park owner's prior written consent to assign the tenancy — but the owner must respond within 10 days of the written request, silence counts as consent given, no fee can be charged for consent, and if consent is unreasonably withheld the home owner can apply for dispute resolution.

faq.q: How much can my pad rent go up each year?
faq.a: Once every 12 months, on at least 3 full months' notice, by no more than the inflation rate (BC consumer price index) plus a proportional amount for the park's changes in local government levies and regulated utilities, divided by the number of sites in the park.

faq.q: What happens to me if the park is sold or redeveloped?
faq.a: For a conversion of all or a significant part of the park, the landlord must have all permits and approvals first, give 12 months' notice, and pay you $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date.

faq.q: How is the purchase actually registered?
faq.a: Through the Manufactured Home Registry — the sale is only effective once registered. Your lawyer or notary files the original signed Bill of Sale and the Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership, and the home must carry its CSA certification label at the point of sale.

faq.q: If I buy a mobile home in a park, do I own the land?
faq.a: No — in a pad-rental park you own the home and rent the site under a pad tenancy agreement; the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on. The exceptions in prove the rule: in a bare-land strata park such as Sea Ridge Bays you own the lot as a strata lot, and in a co-operative such as Pioneer Park the land is held through the co-op.

faq.q: How is financing different for a home on a rented pad?
faq.a: The home is registered in the Manufactured Home Registry rather than dealt with as land title real property, and the transfer is only effective once registered, filed through a lawyer or notary with the signed Bill of Sale and Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership. Lender and mortgage-insurer rules for manufactured homes (chattel vs land-home treatment, age and foundation requirements) were not confirmed on an official source in this research — UNCONFIRMED; confirm financing for the specific home and tenure before removing subjects, and note the extreme case in the Surrey research: a membership (non-strata, non-park) complex whose listing states no mortgages are possible at all.

faq.q: Can the park owner refuse to let me buy a home in the park?
faq.a: The sale needs the park owner's prior written consent to assign the tenancy — but the owner must respond within 10 days of the written request (RTB Form 10), silence counts as consent given, and no fee can be charged for consent. Listings phrase this as "subject to park approval".

faq.q: How much can my pad rent go up each year?
faq.a: Once every 12 months, on at least 3 full months' notice, by no more than the inflation rate (BC consumer price index) plus a proportional amount for the park's changes in local government levies and regulated utilities, divided by the number of sites in the park. For scale, the RTB's own rent-increase form for manufactured home sites states the formula outcome as 3% plus the proportional amount for increases effective in 2025, and 2.3% plus the proportional amount for increases effective in 2026.

faq.q: Can I move my home to another park later?
faq.a: The Act's framework assumes a home can be relocated — the closure-compensation rules even add compensation where a home cannot be moved — but the practical answer depends on the home's age, condition, CSA label and whether another park will accept it, none of which an official source guarantees: UNCONFIRMED for any specific home. What is fixed in law is the paperwork: any later sale or transfer is only effective once registered in the Manufactured Home Registry, and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale — a missing label is a red flag for moving, financing and resale.

faq.q: What happens if the park is sold or redeveloped?
faq.a: A sale of the park alone does not end your tenancy — your assigned tenancy continues on the same terms. A conversion of all or a significant part of the park is different: the landlord must have all permits and approvals first, give 12 months' notice, and pay you $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date; you may leave early on at least 10 days' written notice.

faq.q: Is a park's 55+ age restriction legally valid?
faq.a: Yes, as a park designation under the provincial framework: the Province states that in a designated 55-plus park at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. This is a different legal mechanism from a strata's 55+ bylaw — do not apply strata exemption rules to a pad tenancy; read the park's tenancy agreement and rules, which can state the occupancy rule more strictly.

faq.q: What paperwork should the seller hand me before I write an offer?
faq.a: The written tenancy agreement and the written park rules — the regulation requires the seller to give the proposed purchaser both before the park owner is even asked to consent to the assignment — plus the current pad rent and the date of the last increase, so the increase formula can be checked.

faq.q: Do I pay property tax on a home I own on a rented pad?
faq.a: Yes — a manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential property owners, but the assessed value does not include the value of the land when the home is in a manufactured home park not on reserve land. Some parks include the land portion of property taxes inside the pad rent (Westwood Estates and Val Maria listings both state this) — check what the specific park's pad rent includes.

faq.q: A directory calls a park 55+, but a listing in it says no age restrictions. Which is right?
faq.a: Treat the park as UNCONFIRMED until its own rules settle it — that exact conflict occurred in this research at Breakaway Bays in South Surrey (directory: 55+; MLS listing: "No age or rental restrictions"). Ask the park for its current tenancy agreement and park rules in writing before relying on either claim.
